definitions.definition: Something that exists first and is the foundation for everything else.
definitions.example: If math is ontologically prior to matter, it means math existed before the physical universe and the universe is built on math.

definitions.definition: Two different ways of looking at the same underlying thing.
definitions.example: A 3D object and its shadow are dual projections of the same shape.

definitions.definition: A pattern or set of rules that stays the same even when everything around it changes.
definitions.example: The fact that 2+2=4 is an invariant structure because it's true no matter where you are or what language you speak.

definitions.definition: The belief that abstract ideas like numbers and sets are just names humans made up, not real things that exist on their own.
definitions.example: A nominalist says the number 2 is just a label we use, not a real object floating in space.

definitions.definition: The belief that abstract ideas like numbers and shapes are real things that exist in a non-physical world outside space and time.
definitions.example: A Platonist believes the perfect circle exists somewhere, even though no perfect circle exists in the physical world.

definitions.definition: Something that cannot cause anything to happen or have any effect on the physical world.
definitions.example: A thought is causally inert because thinking about a ball doesn't make it move.

definitions.definition: The belief that mathematical statements are not really true, but we pretend they are because it's useful.
definitions.example: A fictionalist says '2+2=4' is a useful story, not a fact about reality.

definitions.definition: Something that could be different or might not exist at all; depends on something else.
definitions.example: The fact that you are reading this is contingent because you could have chosen to do something else.

definitions.definition: Something that must be true and cannot be false in any possible situation.
definitions.example: 2+2=4 is necessary because there is no possible world where it is false.

definitions.definition: Something that never changes.
definitions.example: The laws of mathematics are immutable because they were the same a billion years ago and will be the same a billion years from now.

definitions.definition: The material or medium something is made of or depends on.
definitions.example: A computer program needs a physical computer as its substrate to run.

definitions.definition: Incapable of being wrong or making mistakes.
definitions.example: If you start with true premises in math, the rules guarantee you will get a true conclusion, so math is infallible.

definitions.definition: When two things are so different they cannot be put in the same group or category.
definitions.example: Calling a banana and a bicycle the same thing is a categorical mismatch because they have almost nothing in common.

definitions.definition: The principle that the simplest explanation with the fewest assumptions is usually the best one.
definitions.example: If you hear hoofbeats, parsimony says think 'horse' not 'zebra' because horses are more common.

definitions.definition: The idea that one kind of thing exists before and is more fundamental than another kind of thing.
definitions.example: If math has ontological priority over matter, then math existed first and matter is built from math.

definitions.definition: The process of writing down a complete set of basic rules (axioms) from which all other truths in a system can be proven.
definitions.example: Euclid wrote down axioms for geometry, which is an early example of formal axiomatization.

definitions.definition: An argument that avoids the real issue by playing with the meaning of words instead of addressing the facts.
definitions.example: Saying 'the sun doesn't rise, the Earth rotates' is a semantic dodge if someone asks why the sun appears to move.

definitions.definition: A specific example or physical version of a general idea or pattern.
definitions.example: A particular red apple is an instantiation of the general concept 'red' and 'apple'.

definitions.definition: Kurt Gödel, a mathematician who proved that in any system of math, there are true statements that cannot be proven within that system.
definitions.example: Gödel showed that math can never be completely self-contained; there will always be unprovable truths.

definitions.definition: Alfred Tarski, a logician who proved that no language can define what 'truth' means within that same language.
definitions.example: Tarski showed that English cannot fully define 'truth' using only English words.

definitions.definition: Alan Turing, a mathematician who proved that there is no general way to know if a computer program will ever finish running or run forever.
definitions.example: Turing showed that you cannot write a program that can always predict whether another program will crash or not.

definitions.definition: The Second Law of Thermodynamics, which says that in a closed system, disorder (entropy) always increases over time and cannot decrease on its own.
definitions.example: An ice cube melts into a puddle because the Second Law says things naturally go from ordered to disordered.

definitions.definition: Rolf Landauer, a physicist who proved that erasing information always produces a tiny amount of heat, so information processing has a physical cost.
definitions.example: Landauer showed that your computer heats up because every time it deletes a file, it releases a tiny bit of heat.

definitions.definition: When multiple independent lines of evidence or reasoning all point to the same conclusion without being designed to do so.
definitions.example: If a detective finds fingerprints, a witness, and a motive all pointing to the same person, that's unforced convergence.

definitions.definition: Specific conditions that, if met, would prove a theory or claim is wrong.
definitions.example: A falsification criterion for 'all swans are white' would be finding a single black swan.

definitions.definition: The ability of something to cause effects or changes in the physical world.
definitions.example: A hammer has causal efficacy because it can drive a nail; a thought does not because thinking about a nail doesn't move it.

definitions.definition: The ability to make choices and take actions intentionally.
definitions.example: A person has agency because they can decide to raise their hand; a rock does not because it cannot choose to move.

definitions.definition: A Greek word (pronounced 'LOH-gos') meaning 'word,' 'reason,' or 'principle' that gives order and meaning to the universe.
definitions.example: In the Bible, Jesus is called the Logos, meaning he is the divine reason that created and sustains everything.

definitions.definition: A made-up term for a rule that says you must state your own belief about where math comes from before you can criticize someone else's view.
definitions.example: The Biaxiosum Rule means you can't say 'math is just invented' without first admitting that view has problems.
